questions.question: What is a median of a random variable $X$?
options: The largest possible value of $X$
A real number $m$ with $P(X\le m)\ge1/2$ and $P(X\ge m)\ge1/2$
The expected squared deviation from the mean
The only value where the density is zero

questions.question: What does a median do conceptually?
options: It splits the distribution into balanced parts
It maximizes the variance
It counts arrivals over time
It gives only the largest observation.

questions.question: Is a median always unique?
options: Yes, every distribution has exactly one median
Only normal distributions have medians
Only discrete distributions have unique medians
No, it need not be unique

questions.question: For a continuous strictly increasing CDF, where is the median?
options: At the point where the CDF equals $1/2$
At the point where the density equals zero
Always at zero
At the maximum of the support only

questions.question: Compared with the mean, how does the median respond to extreme values?
options: It is always more sensitive
It is often less sensitive
It is identical to the maximum
It cannot be computed when extremes exist

questions.question: What is the median of a symmetric normal distribution?
options: Its center
Its variance
Its largest possible value
Its arrival rate

questions.question: For waiting times, what does the median represent?
options: The average of all waiting times necessarily
The last possible waiting time
The time by which half of cases have occurred
The rate of arrivals

questions.question: In income data with extreme high incomes, why might the median describe a typical person better than the mean?
options: It always equals the highest income
It ignores the middle of the distribution
It is computed from variance only
It is less sensitive to extreme high incomes

questions.question: If $F(m)=0.5$ for a continuous strictly increasing CDF, what is $m$?
options: The variance
A median
The mode necessarily
The maximum support point

questions.question: If $P(X\le 4)=0.6$ and $P(X\ge4)=0.7$, is $4$ a median?
options: No, because both probabilities must equal exactly $0.5$
No, because the probabilities are too large
Only if $X$ is normal
Yes

questions.question: Why does the definition use two inequalities instead of only $P(X\le m)=1/2$?
options: It handles jumps and nonunique medians in general distributions
It excludes all discrete distributions
It forces the median to be the mean
It applies only to continuous strictly increasing CDFs

questions.question: How is the median related to the quantile function?
options: It is a variance quantile
It is a $0.5$ quantile
It is always $Q(0.95)$
It is unrelated to distribution positions

questions.question: What does robustness of the median mean here?
options: It never changes under any data change.
It is always equal to the mode
Extreme values affect it less than the mean
It exists only for bounded variables

questions.question: For a distribution with CDF strictly increasing and $F(7)=1/2$, what is the median?
If an income distribution has a few very high values, which center measure is often more typical?
options: Median
Mean only
Variance
Kurtosis

questions.question: If $m$ is a median, what must be true about probability at or below $m$?
options: It is at least $1/2$
It is exactly $0$ always
It is less than $1/2$ always
It equals the variance

questions.question: Why can medians be nonunique for a distribution with a flat CDF region?
options: Flat CDF regions make medians impossible.
Only the mean can be nonunique
A range of values can satisfy the inequalities
The probability total exceeds one

questions.question: What misconception confuses median with mean?
options: Recognizing both are center summaries.
Using the median for income data
Thinking they are equal for every distribution
Calling median a 0.5 quantile

questions.question: If $P(X\le m)=0.4$ and $P(X\ge m)=0.9$, is $m$ a median?
options: Yes, because one side is above $1/2$
Yes, because both probabilities need only be positive
No, the left-side probability is below $1/2$
Only if $m=0$

questions.question: A distribution has every value in $[2,4]$ satisfying the median inequalities. What should be concluded?
options: The distribution has no median
The mean must be $3$
The median must equal the mean
The median is not unique
